To begin, we identify the centroid, or the average, of a set of vectors $\vvec_1, \vvec_2, \ldots,\vvec_n$ as $$ \frac1n\left(\vvec_1+\vvec_2+\ldots+\vvec_n\right). $$

Find the centroid of the vectors $$ \vvec_1=\twovec11, \vvec_2=\twovec41, \vvec_3=\twovec44. $$ and sketch the vectors and the centroid using [fig-centroid-plot]. You may wish to simply plot the points represented by the tips of the vectors rather than drawing the vectors themselves.

The vectors $\vvec_1$, $\vvec_2$, $\vvec_3$ and their centroid.

Notice that the centroid lies in the center of the points defined by the vectors.

Now we'll illustrate an algorithm that forms clusterings. To begin, consider the following points, represented as vectors, $$ \vvec_1=\twovec{-2}{1}, \vvec_2=\twovec11, \vvec_3=\twovec12, \vvec_4=\twovec32, $$ which are shown in [fig-clustering-ex].

We will group this set of four points into two clusters.

Suppose that we would like to group these points into $k=2$ clusters. (Later on, we'll see how to choose an appropriate value for $k$, the number of clusters.) We begin by choosing two points $c_1$ and $c_2$ at random and declaring them to be the centers' of the two clusters.

For example, suppose we randomly choose $c_1=\vvec_2$ and $c_2=\vvec_3$ as the center of two clusters. The cluster centered on $c_1=\vvec_2$ will be the set of points that are closer to $c_1=\vvec_2$ than to $c_2=\vvec_3$. Determine which of the four data points are in this cluster, which we denote by $C_1$, and circle them in [fig-clustering-ex].

The second cluster will consist of the data points that are closer to $c_2=\vvec_3$ than $c_1=\vvec_2$. Determine which of the four points are in this cluster, which we denote by $C_2$, and circle them in [fig-clustering-ex].

We now have a clustering with two clusters, but we will try to improve upon it in the following way. First, find the centroids of the two clusters; that is, redefine $c_1$ to be the centroid of cluster $C_1$ and $c_2$ to be the centroid of $C_2$. Find those centroids and indicate them in [fig-clustering-ex-2]

Indicate the new centroids and clusters.

Now update the cluster $C_1$ to be the set of points closer to $c_1$ than $c_2$. Update the cluster $C_2$ in a similar way and indicate the clusters in [fig-clustering-ex-2].

Let's perform this last step again. That is, update the centroids $c_1$ and $c_2$ from the new clusters and then update the clusters $C_1$ and $C_2$. Indicate your centroids and clusters in [fig-clustering-ex-3].

Indicate the new centroids and clusters.

Notice that this last step produces the same set of clusters so there is no point in repeating it. We declare this to be our final clustering.
